blocks.text: Ooh, which vase would you choose? I’m usually caught by the color first, then I start following the curve and wondering about the hands behind it. At Cincinnati’s Rookwood Pottery, that curiosity takes us back to 1880. Pick a piece you like. We can start with your favorite instead of mine. ♡

blocks.title: Art for the room you live in

blocks.text: Maria Longworth Nichols Storer founded Rookwood in Cincinnati in 1880. The pottery’s history begins with a former schoolhouse, Ohio River clay, and a single kiln. Imagine starting there, with a material that can become a cup, a tile, or something made simply because you want to see its shape. It’s an inviting place to begin a making story.

I’d look in three little passes: outline, surface, then the place where the glaze gathers or changes. Rookwood’s early artists worked with individual designs, form, decoration, and glaze. Giving each choice a moment helps me notice more than just ‘ooh, pretty.’ Though, honestly, that’s a lovely place to start.

blocks.title: A piece passes from hand to hand

blocks.text: Ready for the part that surprised me in Rookwood’s own description? A piece passes through at least thirteen sets of hands. Shaping, finishing, glazing, and firing call for different kinds of attention. Clay also changes while it dries and fires. The work has pauses in it; a fresh form can’t be rushed straight to the table.

A tile asks us to step back a little. Rookwood still makes architectural tile and custom work, so one small surface might become part of an entire room. Look at how neighboring pieces repeat a color or pattern. With a vase, you can walk around the object. With a tiled wall, the object is all around you.

blocks.title: First the shape, then the glaze
blocks.text: A Rookwood piece brings choices of form, decoration, and glaze together. I’m usually drawn to the color first, then the place where it gathers along an edge. Show me your favorite detail? I like seeing what I missed through your eyes. ♡

blocks.title: Look across time, then look again

blocks.text: To see how those choices change over time, look through museum collections and Rookwood’s own history. Compare an older piece with something made today. You might notice a familiar approach to color or a completely different shape. Let one detail catch your attention before reading its label; then see what the maker or museum can tell you about it.

For a Cincinnati visit, check Rookwood’s current shop hours and factory-tour arrangements. A shop visit and a collection offer different ways to meet the work. I’d choose whichever gives us time to linger over one piece. A cup can hold a surprisingly long conversation. ♡
